title: Per-object scenes: PlayCanvas carries twice the load
body: With 5,000 individually animated meshes on WebGPU, PlayCanvas spends 12 ms of CPU per frame, Babylon.js 24 ms and three.js 29 ms (Chrome). The largest such scene each engine keeps inside a 60 fps frame is about 6,300 meshes for PlayCanvas, 3,200 for Babylon.js and 2,800 for three.js. PlayCanvas leads in every browser; second place changes, and Babylon.js drops below 1,000 meshes in Safari.

title: Instancing makes the engine choice almost irrelevant
body: Through each engine's own fast path (three.js InstancedMesh, PlayCanvas hardware instancing, Babylon.js thin instances), 50,000 animated meshes cost 1.1–2.3 ms of CPU on WebGPU in Chrome. That is less than any naive path spends on 5,000. Every engine sustains all 50,000 at 60 fps in every browser, so whether a scene can be instanced matters more than which engine draws it.

title: WebGPU isn't automatically faster
body: On the naive per-object scene, PlayCanvas and Babylon.js ran faster on their WebGL2 backends than on WebGPU in Chrome (7.5 vs 12 ms and 19 vs 24 ms at 5,000 meshes). three.js's classic WebGLRenderer, at 7.3 ms, beat its own WebGPURenderer at 29 ms. WebGPU pays off on the instanced paths: 50,000 meshes cost 1.1–2.3 ms there versus 3.9–6.7 ms on WebGL2.

title: Forward lighting: PlayCanvas barely notices 32 lights
body: With 32 moving point lights and no clustering, PlayCanvas renders a frame in 1.3 ms of GPU time against 53 ms for three.js (Chrome), for the same image. PlayCanvas's shader skips any light whose attenuation is zero at the pixel. Babylon.js can't run this path on WebGPU at all: each forward light takes its own uniform buffer, and the per-stage limit leaves room for 8 in Chrome (27 in Firefox). In Safari, WebKit rejects three.js's 32-light shader (private shader memory is capped at 8 KB) and nothing renders.

title: Shadows: PlayCanvas is 2.5–4× lighter on the CPU
body: Rendering 2,000 animated meshes with a 4-cascade sun and four shadow-casting spot lights costs PlayCanvas 21 ms of CPU per frame, three.js 52 ms and Babylon.js 78 ms on WebGPU in Chrome. GPU time differs far less (8–21 ms), so the gap is on the CPU side. Adding bloom and ACES leaves the CPU cost almost unchanged but raises GPU time, most for three.js (21 → 51 ms) and PlayCanvas (8 → 20 ms).

title: Babylon.js pays a heavy Safari tax
body: three.js and PlayCanvas cost about the same CPU in Safari as in Chrome. Babylon.js's per-object path does not: 5,000 meshes cost it 103 ms in Safari versus 24 ms in Chrome, and the shadow scene 226 ms versus 78 ms. Its instanced paths stay fast everywhere.

title: Skinning and compute are a wash; Babylon.js has the only skinning fast path
body: Five hundred walking Fox characters cost 12–14 ms of CPU in Chrome in all three engines, and a million compute-simulated particles take about 7 ms of GPU time in each. Babylon.js's baked vertex animation is the only built-in fast path that keeps each character's own animation phase, and it cuts those 500 characters to 0.1 ms of CPU.

title: Startup: three.js is smallest, Babylon.js slowest to first frame
body: A minimal lit-cube app ships 166 KB of brotli-compressed JavaScript with three.js, 202 KB with PlayCanvas and 279 KB with Babylon.js (104 KB with three.js's classic WebGLRenderer). In Chrome, three.js and PlayCanvas reach their first WebGPU frame in about 100 ms. Babylon.js takes 330 ms, largely because it fetches its shader code on first use.

title: Each browser's WebGPU has its own sharp edges
body: Firefox 150 loses the GPU device when render passes carry timestamp writes, so it reports no GPU time here. Safari caps frames at the display rate. It also rejects shaders with large private arrays, and three.js's compileAsync never resolves there for scenes with many meshes. Chrome lets JavaScript run far ahead of the GPU when uncapped. None of this shows up in a single-browser benchmark.
